1) a compound with **-pijn**, no article: *Ik heb **hoofdpijn / keelpijn / buikpijn / kiespijn**.* 2) **pijn in** + body part: *Ik heb pijn in mijn rug.* 3) **doet pijn / doet zeer**: *Mijn knie doet pijn.* Longer trouble: **last hebben van**: *Ik heb last van mijn rug.*

**Hoe lang heb je dat al?** — How long have you had it? Dutch uses the **present** + **al** or **sinds**: *Ik **ben al** drie dagen ziek.* (I've been ill for three days.) *Ik **heb sinds** maandag koorts.*

to go; to be going to

Good morning. Here is the weather forecast for today and tomorrow. Today it is cloudy and rainy. In the west it's going to rain all day. There's a strong wind and it won't get warmer than twelve degrees. So take an umbrella with you if you go out. Tomorrow will be better. In the morning there will still be some fog, but in the afternoon the sun will shine. It will be about eighteen degrees. At the weekend it will stay dry and sunny, so it's nice weather for cycling or walking.

*Het is **warm / koud / heet / koel / nat / droog**.* *Het is **zonnig / bewolkt / winderig / regenachtig**.* *Het is **mooi / lekker / slecht** weer.* Temperature: *Het is **twintig graden**.* *Het is **min vijf**.*

**Wat voor weer is het?** — What's the weather like? **Hoe warm is het?** — How warm is it? **Wat een weer!** — What weather! (usually bad). The Dutch love talking about the weather — it changes all the time.

The most common way: *Morgen **werk** ik niet.* *Volgende week **ben** ik in Parijs.* *Zaterdag **wordt** het mooi weer.*
For plans and things about to happen — like English “going to”. The infinitive goes to the **end**: *Ik **ga** morgen **fietsen**.* *Het **gaat regenen**.* *Wat **ga** je dit weekend **doen**?*

**zullen** is for promises, predictions and suggestions: *Ik **zal** je morgen bellen.* (promise) *Het **zal** morgen wel regenen.* (probably) ***Zullen** we naar het strand gaan?* (Shall we…?) Forms: ik zal, jij zult/zal, hij zal, wij zullen.

omdat, dat, als: the verb goes to the end

After **omdat** (because), **dat** (that), **als** (if/when), **wanneer** (when) and **of** (whether), the conjugated **verb goes to the END** of the clause: *Ik blijf thuis, **omdat** het **regent**.* *Ik denk **dat** hij ziek **is**.* *Ik weet niet **of** hij **komt**.*

Both mean “because”, but **want** is followed by normal word order, **omdat** sends the verb to the end: *Ik blijf thuis, **want** het **regent** hard.* = *Ik blijf thuis, **omdat** het hard **regent**.* The same with **en, maar, of (or), dus**: normal order.
With a modal, both verbs are at the end: *…, omdat ik morgen **moet werken**.* A separable verb joins up again: *Ik denk dat ik mijn paraplu **meeneem**.* (main clause: *Ik neem mijn paraplu mee.*)
If the sub-clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb: ***Als het regent**, **gaan** we naar de bioscoop.* (verb – comma – verb).

When I was little: the simple past

When I was little, we lived in a village in the north of the Netherlands. My grandpa and grandma had a farm there. I had a dog, Bobbie, and two cats. Every day I cycled to primary school, even when it rained. After school I played outside with my friends. We had no computer and no mobile phone, but we were never indoors. In summer we swam in the lake and in winter we could sometimes skate. When I was twelve, we moved to the city, because my father got a job there. At first I thought that was terrible, but later it became fun. I still often think of the village.

Last year we went to Italy by car. The trip took two days. The first night we slept in a small hotel in Switzerland. The view of the mountains was beautiful. The next day we arrived at the campsite late in the evening. We were very tired, but we still had to put up the tent first. The first week the weather was great. We swam in the lake every day, ate pizza and ice cream and took lots of photos. But then it suddenly started to rain. It rained for three days and everything in the tent got wet. Luckily we found a hotel in the village. We stayed there until the end of the holiday. It wasn't cheap, but it was dry!
The simple past of zijn and hebben
The simple past (*imperfectum*) has one form for the singular and one for the plural — much easier than the present.

For descriptions, habits and situations in the past: *Vroeger **had** ik lang haar.* *Het **was** koud.* *Als kind **was** ik vaak ziek.* With *zijn* and *hebben* the simple past is far more common than the perfect: say *Ik **was** gisteren thuis*, not *Ik ben thuis geweest*.
**Vroeger** woonde ik in Utrecht. — I used to live in Utrecht. Ik woon er **nog steeds**. — I still live there. Ik woon er **niet meer**. — I don't live there any more. *Ik ben **geboren** in 1995.*

Take the stem (the *ik*-form). Singular: stem + **te** or **de**. Plural: stem + **ten** or **den**. *werken → ik **werkte**, wij **werkten*** · *wonen → ik **woonde**, wij **woonden***.
't kofschip — the same rule as for the participle
If the stem (infinitive minus -en) ends in **t, k, f, s, ch, p** → **-te**: *maakte, fietste, kookte, wachtte, praatte*. Otherwise → **-de**: *speelde, hoorde, belde, leerde, regende*.
v and z in the infinitive
Look at the infinitive, not the *ik*-form: *rei**z**en → ik reis → ik **reisde*** (z → -de) · *verhui**z**en → **verhuisde*** · *le**v**en → **leefde***.

If the stem already ends in t or d, you get two: *wachten → **wachtte***, *praten → **praatte***, *antwoorden → **antwoordde***. It sounds the same as the present plural, but the spelling is different.

Strong verbs change their vowel and take **no ending** in the singular; the plural adds **-en**: *ik **ging**, wij **gingen*** · *ik **kwam**, wij **kwamen*** · *ik **zag**, wij **zagen***. You have to learn them — but they are the most frequent verbs in the language.
A small group changes the stem and ends in **-cht / -st**: *kopen → **kocht***, *brengen → **bracht***, *denken → **dacht***, *weten → **wist***. And *zeggen → **zei** (zeiden)*.
Notice the spelling: *ik **at*** (short a) → *wij **aten*** (long a); *ik **las*** → *wij **lazen***; *ik **gaf*** → *wij **gaven***. The plural has a long vowel and s/f become z/v.

toen, and the past of modal verbs

As a conjunction **toen** means “when” for the past, and — like *omdat* — it sends the verb to the end: ***Toen** ik klein **was**, woonden we in een dorp.* For the present, the future or a repeated event use **als**: *Als ik moe ben, ga ik vroeg slapen.*

As an adverb **toen** means “then” and causes inversion: *Ik at een boterham. **Toen ging** ik naar mijn werk.* Other story words: **eerst** (first), **daarna** (after that), **plotseling** (suddenly), **ten slotte** (finally).
In the past, modal verbs are almost always used in the simple past, not the perfect.

**Perfect** for a single finished event, especially in conversation: *Ik **heb** gisteren een boek **gekocht**.* **Simple past** for descriptions, habits and a chain of events in a story: *Het **was** koud. We **liepen** naar huis en **dronken** thee.* Typical: start with the perfect, continue in the simple past.

At home: rooms, furniture, er, renting a flat

For rent: bright and spacious flat on the third floor, close to the centre of Utrecht. The flat is 65 square metres. There is a large living room with a balcony, a modern kitchen with a fridge, an oven and a dishwasher, and there are two bedrooms. In the bathroom there is a shower and a washing machine. There is no bath. The flat is unfurnished. The rent is 1,250 euros a month, excluding gas, water and electricity. The deposit is two months' rent. The neighbourhood is quiet and there are lots of shops. The bus stop is opposite the building. Viewing on Saturday between ten and twelve.

I've finally found a room! It isn't big, but it is cosy. When you come in, my bed is on the left. Next to the bed there is a small table with a lamp. Opposite the bed there is a big wardrobe. My clothes hang in it. Under the window is my desk. My laptop is always on it, and there are also lots of books and papers. On the wall there are photos of my family and a painting by my sister. On the floor there is a red rug. There are three plants in front of the window. Yesterday I bought a mirror. I hung it next to the door. I share the kitchen and the bathroom with two other students. They're nice, but they never tidy up!

To say that something exists, start with **er**: ***Er is** een balkon.* (There is a balcony.) ***Er zijn** twee slaapkamers.* (There are two bedrooms.) Negative with **geen**: *Er is **geen** bad.* Question: ***Is er** een tuin?*
*er is* introduces something new (een, geen, a number, veel): *Er is **een** keuken.* For something already known, no *er*: ***De** keuken is klein.*

**de begane grond** = ground floor; **de eerste verdieping** = one floor up (the *second* floor for Russian speakers!). *Ik woon **op** de derde verdieping.* **boven** — upstairs, **beneden** — downstairs: *De slaapkamers zijn boven.*

Putting things: zetten, leggen, stoppen, hangen
Each position verb has a partner for *putting* something there. The result of **zetten** is that it **staat**; the result of **leggen** is that it **ligt**.

**zetten – zette – gezet**, **leggen – legde – gelegd**, **stoppen – stopte – gestopt** (regular), **hangen – hing – gehangen** (irregular). Position verbs are all irregular: *staan – stond – gestaan*, *liggen – lag – gelegen*, *zitten – zat – gezeten*.
*de tv **aan**zetten / **uit**zetten* (switch on / off) · *koffie **zetten*** (make coffee) · *iets **neer**zetten / **neer**leggen* (put down) · *de was in de wasmachine **doen***.

er: the little word that is everywhere
1. er is / er zijn — there is
*Er is een probleem.* *Er staan drie planten voor het raam.* *Er woont een student boven.* — with any verb, when the subject is indefinite.
*Ken je Utrecht? — Ja, ik woon **er** al tien jaar.* (= in Utrecht) *Ik ben **er** nog nooit geweest.* With stress use **daar**: *Dáár woon ik!*

When you count without repeating the noun, Dutch needs **er**: *Hoeveel kamers heb je? — Ik heb **er** twee.* *Heb je kinderen? — Ja, ik heb **er** drie.* *Ik heb **er** geen.* (Russian: «у меня их две».)

Instead of *preposition + het/hem* for things, use **er + preposition**: *Ik kijk naar het programma. → Ik kijk **ernaar**.* *Ik denk **eraan**.* *De laptop ligt **erop**.* Often split: *Ik heb **er** lang **op** gewacht.*

Many household verbs are separable: **schoonmaken** → *Ik **maak** de keuken **schoon**.* → *Ik heb de keuken **schoongemaakt**.* **opruimen** → *Ruim je kamer **op**!* → ***opgeruimd***. **afwassen** → *Wie **wast af**?* → ***afgewassen***. But **stofzuigen** is not separable: *Ik **stofzuig** → **gestofzuigd***.

**moeten** = must: *Ik moet nog strijken.* The negative “don't have to” is **hoeven niet … te**: *Je **hoeft** vandaag **niet te** koken.* *Je **hoeft niets** mee **te** nemen.* (*Je moet niet koken* means “you mustn't”.)

Use **u** with strangers, older people, customers and in formal letters. The verb takes the *jij*-form with -t, also in questions: *U **werkt** hier.* → ***Werkt** u hier?* (compare *Werk je hier?*). **zijn** and **hebben**: *u bent, u hebt / heeft*. Possessive: **uw** naam. *Alsjeblieft → **alstublieft***.

**zou / zouden** makes a request softer: ***Zou** u mij **kunnen** helpen?* — Could you help me? ***Zou** ik iets **mogen** vragen?* — Might I ask something? *Ik **zou graag** een afspraak **willen** maken.* — I would like to make an appointment.
Small words make Dutch friendlier: **even** (just, briefly), **misschien** (perhaps), **graag** (gladly). *Kunt u **even** wachten?* *Hebt u **misschien** een pen?* *Ja, **graag**!* — Yes, please!
Dutch people switch to *je/jij* quickly, especially at work. They may say: *Zeg maar **je**, hoor!* — Just say *je*. In shops and on the phone with companies, start with *u*.

A relative clause tells you *which* person or thing. Use **die** for **de**-words and all plurals, **dat** for **het**-words in the singular: *de man **die** daar staat* · *de boeken **die** ik lees* · *het huis **dat** te koop is* · *het meisje **dat** hier werkt*.
It is a sub-clause, so the verb goes to the end: *Dat is de vrouw **die** hier **werkt**.* *Dit is het boek **dat** ik gisteren **heb gekocht**.* The clause comes right after the noun.
With a preposition, for people: met wie

For people after a preposition use **wie**: *de collega **met wie** ik werk* · *de man **op wie** ik wacht*. For things use **waar + preposition**: *het bedrijf **waar** ik **voor** werk* · *de stoel **waarop** ik zit*.
Don't mix up the two dat's
*Ik denk **dat** hij komt.* — conjunction “that” (always dat). *Het boek **dat** ik lees.* — relative pronoun (dat only for het-words; *de krant **die** ik lees*).

Pancakes are typically Dutch and very easy to make. For eight pancakes you need: 250 grams of flour, two eggs, half a litre of milk, a little salt and butter for frying.

Put the flour and the salt in a bowl. Add the eggs and half of the milk. Stir well until there are no more lumps. Then pour in the rest of the milk and stir again. Heat a little butter in a frying pan. Pour a thin layer of batter into the pan. Fry the pancake for about two minutes on each side, until it is golden brown. Serve the pancakes warm.

In the Netherlands pancakes are often eaten with syrup or sugar, but also with cheese or bacon. They are usually eaten in the evening, not for breakfast. Enjoy!

Many cookbooks and packets use the infinitive at the end: *De uien **snijden**. Tien minuten **koken**. Goed **roeren**.* Both styles mean the same.

After a measure there is **no preposition**: *200 **gram meel*** · *een **liter melk*** · *een **glas water*** · *twee **eetlepels olie*** · *een **stuk kaas*** · *een **plak ham***. And **gram, kilo, liter** stay singular after a number: *drie **kilo** aardappelen*.

**een beetje** zout (a little) · **genoeg** (enough) · **te veel / te weinig** (too much / too little) · **ongeveer** tien minuten (about) · **een halve** liter · **anderhalve** liter (one and a half).

When the action matters more than who does it, use **worden** + participle (at the end): *Kaas **wordt** van melk **gemaakt**.* — Cheese is made from milk. *Hier **wordt** Nederlands **gesproken**.* *De pannenkoeken **worden** warm **geserveerd**.*
The doer can be added with **door**: *Het eten wordt **door** de kok gemaakt.* Active: *De kok maakt het eten.*

*Het huis **werd** in 1920 **gebouwd**.* — The house was built in 1920. *De gasten **werden** hartelijk **ontvangen**.* For a finished result Dutch uses **zijn**: *Het huis **is gebouwd** in 1920.* *De winkel **is gesloten**.*

Dutch loves the impersonal passive: ***Er wordt** veel gefietst in Nederland.* — People cycle a lot. ***Er wordt** gebeld.* — Someone's at the door / the phone is ringing. Russian would say «много ездят», «звонят».

For going to do an activity: *Ik **ga zwemmen**.* *We **gaan** zaterdag **wandelen**.* **hardlopen** is special: *Ik **loop hard*** (separable) or simply *Ik **ga hardlopen***.

Sport in the Netherlands is organised in clubs: *Ik **ben lid van** een tennisclub.* *Ik **zit op** voetbal / yoga / dansen.* (I do… at a club) *We **trainen** twee keer per week.* *Zaterdag hebben we **een wedstrijd**.*

To stress that something is happening right now: *Ik **ben aan het koken**.* — I'm cooking. *Wat **ben** je **aan het doen**?* *De kinderen **zijn** buiten **aan het spelen**.* The object goes before *aan het*: *Ik ben **een boek** aan het lezen.*

The simple present can also mean “now”: *Ik **kook**.* The *aan het* form is used when you really mean “in the middle of it”. It is not used with verbs of state: say *Ik **woon** in Utrecht*, never *ik ben aan het wonen*.
Very Dutch: use the body position + **te** + infinitive. *Ik **zit te lezen**.* (I'm reading — sitting.) *Hij **staat te wachten**.* *Ze **ligt te slapen**.* *We **lopen te praten**.*
*Ik **was aan het koken** toen je belde.* — I was cooking when you called. *We **zaten te eten**.* **bezig zijn met**: *Ik **ben bezig met** mijn huiswerk.*
*Ik wil **fit blijven**.* *Ik heb **een goede / slechte conditie**.* *Je moet meer **bewegen**.* (exercise more) *Ik wil vijf kilo **afvallen**.* *Ik heb **een blessure** aan mijn knie.*

To give a purpose: *Ik sport **om** fit **te blijven**.* — I do sport to stay fit. *Ik ga naar de markt **om** groente **te kopen**.* Everything stands between *om* and *te*; the infinitive comes last. Separable verbs: *om **op te** staan*, *om mee **te** gaan* → written *om mee te gaan*.

Some verbs take **te** + infinitive: **proberen** (try), **beginnen** (begin), **vergeten** (forget), **besluiten** (decide), **beloven** (promise), **hopen**, **hoeven niet**. *Ik **probeer** elke dag **te** lezen.* *Hij **vergat** de deur dicht **te** doen.* *Het **begint te** regenen.*
No *te* after modal verbs and *gaan, komen, blijven, laten, zien, horen*: *Ik **wil** zwemmen.* *Ik **ga** zwemmen.* *Kom je **eten**?* *Ik **blijf** zitten.* *Ik **laat** mijn fiets **repareren**.*

*Ik **heb zin om** uit **te** gaan.* (feel like) · *Ik **ben van plan om** te verhuizen.* (intend) · *Het is **leuk / moeilijk / gezond om** … **te** …*: *Het is gezond **om** veel **te** bewegen.* · *Ik heb **geen tijd om te** sporten.*

She tries to do sport three times a week.

*Ja, **leuk**!* · ***Graag!*** · *Goed idee!* · *Dat **lijkt me leuk**.* (That sounds fun.) · ***Afgesproken!*** (Agreed!) · *Hoe laat **spreken we af**?* · *Waar **zullen we afspreken**?*

2. The rest of the verb goes to the end
Infinitives, participles and separable prefixes close the sentence: *Ik **wil** morgen vroeg **opstaan**.* · *Ik **heb** gisteren een boek **gekocht**.* · *Ik **sta** elke dag om zeven uur **op**.*
3. Sub-clause: all verbs at the end

After **omdat, dat, als, toen, of, wanneer, terwijl, hoewel** and after **die / dat**: *…, omdat ik moe **ben**.* · *…, dat hij morgen **komt**.* · *…, omdat ik vroeg **moet opstaan**.* · *de man die hier **werkt***.

In the middle of the sentence the usual order is **time → manner → place**: *Ik ga **morgen** **met de trein** **naar Utrecht**.* And *niet* comes before the place or adjective: *Ik ga morgen **niet** naar Utrecht.*
